content.text: In a parallel circuit, components are connected across each other—there are multiple paths for current to flow. This is how most household wiring works: each appliance has its own path to the supply, so if one fails, the others continue working. Understanding parallel circuits is essential for electrical engineering and everyday safety.
In a parallel circuit: potential difference is the same across each branch, current splits between branches, and total resistance is less than the smallest individual resistance.
, components are connected across each other, providing multiple paths for current.
Each component has its own path from positive to negative
Each branch experiences the full supply voltage
If one branch fails, others continue working

content.text: The p.d. is the SAME across all branches.
Why? Each branch connects directly to the supply terminals.
The total current equals the SUM of currents in each branch.
The current splits at junctions and recombines when branches meet.
This is Kirchhoff's Current Law: current in = current out at any junction.

content.text: Every socket in your home is wired in parallel to the mains supply. This is why you can switch a kettle off without turning off the lights — each appliance operates independently.
— True for series, but in parallel, adding resistors DECREASES total resistance.
"Current is the same in all branches"
— Current splits according to resistance. Lower resistance = more current.
— Total parallel resistance is always LESS than the smallest individual resistor.
— Components can be drawn anywhere but are parallel if they share the same two nodes (connection points).
— Breaking one branch in parallel just stops current in that branch; others continue.
